sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Go passes arguments by value. Passing a struct copies that struct value; passing a pointer copies an address that can refer to the same underlying object.

A value receiver gets a copy of the receiver, while a pointer receiver can modify fields of the original value. Reference-like fields such as slices and maps can still share underlying data inside a copied struct.

For example, `func (c *Counter) Increment()` changes the caller's `Counter`. The value-receiver form increments only its local copy, so the caller sees no field change.

Pointers do not automatically make code faster, and pointer use does not by itself prove heap allocation. Escape analysis and compiler decisions determine storage.

Use a pointer receiver when a method must mutate the receiver, when copying the value would be undesirable, or when receiver consistency and method-set requirements call for it.

sections.title: The core model: pointer and value choices in Go
sections.content:
pointer and value choices in Go is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

Copying an integer duplicates its bits. Copying a struct duplicates each field value. If a field is a slice header, map descriptor, pointer, channel, or function, the copied descriptor can still refer to the same underlying resource. 'Value copy' therefore does not always mean independent deep data.

sections.title: The practical decision: pointer and value choices in Go
sections.content:
The useful question is not whether pointer and value choices in Go can be used, but which requirement makes it the clearest and safest fit. That decision includes its cost and its failure boundary.

Mutation is the strongest reason for a pointer receiver. Large values, types containing synchronization primitives, and types defined around identity also favour pointers. Small immutable value types can use value receivers naturally. Consistency helps users know what copying the type means.

sections.title: Why the failure happens: pointer and value choices in Go
sections.content:
Failures around pointer and value choices in Go usually come from one incorrect assumption about ownership, state, ordering, or lifetime. Finding that assumption is more useful than adding a defensive line at random.

A value method can change its local field and appear to work while logging inside the method, yet the caller's field remains unchanged. Conversely, changing an element through a slice field may affect shared storage even on a value receiver. Tests should cover both top-level fields and referenced contents.

sections.title: The important trade-off: pointer and value choices in Go
sections.content:
pointer and value choices in Go and using the other receiver or parameter form solve related problems, but they expose different guarantees. The best choice follows from the guarantee the program actually needs.

Method sets matter at interface assignment. If an interface requires `Save()` and only `func (*Record) Save()` exists, a `Record` value does not implement it while `*Record` does. Calls on addressable values may receive automatic `&` convenience, but interface satisfaction follows the formal method set.

sections.title: A reliable diagnosis: pointer and value choices in Go
sections.content:
A good investigation traces the first point where the real state differs from the expected state. With pointer and value choices in Go, that means observing the relevant input, transition, and result rather than guessing from the final symptom.

For a new type, write down whether zero is useful, nil is valid, copies should be independent, and methods mutate identity. A mutex-bearing type should not be copied after use. For concurrent mutable state, pointer semantics also require an explicit synchronization policy.
